measure.title: CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.

terms.plain: The middle income level among local families, with half earning more and half earning less.
The part of a home's price a buyer pays up front instead of financing with the main mortgage.
Borrowing that is repaid from specified payments, such as borrowers' loan payments.
The loan's interest rate stays the same rather than changing over time.
A problem with how a home was built that may violate required building standards.
Lawyers' fees paid as a share of the money recovered for their clients.
The income level in the middle of a local area's income distribution, adjusted for household size.

summary.text: Creates a **loan program** for middle-income buyers of new homes.
summary.more: The loan program—legally the Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program—finances up to 17% of a home's price. Buyers must contribute at least 3%, occupy the home, and earn no more than twice local median family income for their family size.

quotes.text: Establish middle-class home ownership loans to make home financing more affordable for the purchase of a newly constructed single-family home, with no cost to taxpayers. … “Program” means the Middle-Class Home Ownership Loan Program.

shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment, where the applicant contributes no less than 3 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home.

The applicant shall agree to occupy the qualified new home as the applicant’s primary residence within 60 days of closing. … The applicant shall have a family income that does not exceed 200 percent of the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area where the qualified new home is located, adjusted for family size by the agency. … The applicant shall agree to pay no less than 3 percent of the purchase price of the qualified new home from a source other than a grant or borrowed money.

background.text: A down payment is the part of a home's price buyers pay up front. California's housing finance agency already offers loans to help eligible buyers make that payment; those loans must be repaid.

quotes.text: When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front—typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment.
CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.

nodes.label: A second loan for part of the purchase
nodes.title: A second mortgage could finance **up to 17 percent** of a qualified new home's price

quotes.text: Each middle-class home ownership loan shall be secured by a secondary mortgage, shall be used solely … to finance a portion of the purchase price of a qualified new home, and shall finance no more than 17 percent of the purchase price of a qualified new home that is ordinarily covered by the homeowner’s downpayment,

nodes.label: Residency, income, occupancy and savings
nodes.title: Buyers must meet **residency, income and down payment requirements** and live in the home

quotes.text: be a resident of the State of California for at least one year prior to the time of application. … applicant’s primary residence within 60 days of closing. … family income that does not exceed 200 percent of the area median income for a family of the same size in the county or metropolitan statistical area where the qualified new home is located, adjusted for family size by the agency. … agree to pay no less than 3 percent of the purchase price of the qualified new home from a source other than a grant or borrowed money.

nodes.label: New homes and converted residential units
nodes.title: Eligible homes must have a **first purchaser** and meet a locally indexed price limit

quotes.text: A newly constructed home, townhome, row house, condominium, or manufactured home where the borrower is the first purchaser. … A condominium or other residential unit in a building that was a nonresidential structure and was retrofitted or repurposed for residential use where the borrower is the first purchaser. … The maximum sales price for a qualified new home shall not exceed 125 percent of the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in the county in which the qualified new home is located,

nodes.label: Revenue bonds fund the program
nodes.title: The housing agency could issue **up to $25 billion** in revenue bonds, excluding refunding bonds

quotes.text: provided that the principal amount of any bonds issued and sold pursuant to this chapter shall not exceed twenty-five billion dollars ($25,000,000,000), not including the amount of any refunding bonds issued pursuant to paragraph (2).

nodes.label: Loan terms must cover program obligations
nodes.title: Loan payments are intended to cover **bond repayment and administration**

quotes.text: agency determines practical and favorable to applicants … and at levels necessary, to the greatest extent possible, to pay the principal, interest, and other amounts due with respect to the bonds issued pursuant to this chapter, including amounts necessary to defray all costs of administration incurred by the agency pursuant to this chapter.

nodes.label: Fixed rates and no early payment penalties
nodes.title: Loans must be **fixed-rate**, with lender fee limits and no early payment penalties

quotes.text: Limits on lenders fees associated with the origination of middle-class home ownership loans. … A prohibition on early payment penalties. … A requirement that middle-class home ownership loans be fixed-rate mortgage loans.

nodes.label: Optional builder participation
nodes.title: Builders may choose an **optional participation route** with specified labor obligations

quotes.text: A housing developer may voluntarily opt into the option by certifying to the agency that the construction of a new home or homes will satisfy the requirements established in subdivision (b) of Section 51515.01.

Be subject to the labor and enforcement provisions in paragraphs (2), (3), if the project and construction craft conditions specified in that paragraph are met, (4), and (5) of subdivision (d) of Section 21080.66 of the Public Resources Code.

nodes.label: Changes to repair claims and lawyer fees
nodes.title: Construction defect claims face **changed procedures**, including limits on contingency fees

quotes.text: written notice required shall identify each homeowner by address or other description sufficient to apprise the builder of the location of each residence, shall identify the nature and location of each alleged violation in each residence, and shall be signed by each homeowner alleging a violation.

The homeowner may voluntarily execute a release of claims related solely to the repaired deficiencies. That release shall be in writing, executed knowingly and voluntarily, and shall not extend to any defects or claims not addressed by the repairs.

the maximum allowable attorney contingency fee shall not exceed 30 percent of the total recovery obtained through settlement, mediation, arbitration, judicial reference, or judgment, unless a court approves a higher award

nodes.label: Independent annual audit
nodes.title: An **independent annual audit** must check how bond proceeds are used

quotes.text: The agency shall provide for an independent annual audit of the program to ensure that bond proceeds are used in a manner consistent with the requirements of this chapter and any other applicable laws.

nodes.label: Implementation deadline
nodes.title: The agency must implement the program **within one year** after the act takes effect

quotes.text: The agency shall implement the program no later than one year after the effective date of this act.

nodes.label: Down payments keep workers from buying
nodes.title: Workers who can afford monthly mortgages are blocked by **down payment requirements**

quotes.locator: Argument in favor, paragraph beginning 'Teachers, nurses'
quotes.text: Teachers, nurses, veterans, and firefighters work hard and pay their bills. They can afford monthly mortgage payments but are locked out of homeownership in the communities where they live and work because down payment requirements are too high.

quotes.text: Homebuyers must qualify for a mortgage, meet income requirements, pay at least 3% down, occupy the home as their primary residence, make monthly payments, and fully repay their loans.

nodes.label: Help for working families between programs
nodes.title: The loans would help families who earn too much for rental aid but **cannot save a down payment**

quotes.locator: Argument in favor, KEEPING HOMEOWNERSHIP WITHIN REACH
quotes.text: Prop. 37 is designed for renters, first-time homebuyers, and working families who earn too much to qualify for renter assistance programs, but not enough to save the massive down payment required to buy a home.

quotes.text: Proposition 37 is supported by Democrats & Republicans, labor and businesses, construction workers, taxpayer and housing advocates, veterans, the California Teachers Association, and United Nurses Association of California.

nodes.label: No direct state or local costs
nodes.title: Borrower payments mean **no direct state or local costs**

quotes.locator: FISCAL EFFECTS, No Direct State or Local Costs
quotes.text: Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.

nodes.label: Investor demand and loan costs remain unknown
nodes.title: The program's impact depends on **investor demand, loan costs and construction response**

quotes.text: A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.

nodes.label: Higher labor standards, more builder flexibility
nodes.title: Optional higher labor standards come with **more flexible construction defect rules** for builders

quotes.text: Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.

nodes.label: Low interest must coexist with repayment
nodes.title: Loan payments must cover program costs while **interest costs stay as low as possible**

quotes.locator: PROPOSAL, Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program
quotes.text: Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible.

nodes.label: Existing construction standards and claims process
nodes.title: Existing law requires **building standards and a pre-lawsuit process** for construction defect claims

quotes.text: To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards.

nodes.label: Other assistance loans already exist
nodes.title: The state housing agency already offers **repayable down payment assistance**

quotes.text: CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.

nodes.label: No published argument against

quotes.text: NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

nodes.title: The implementation deadline is **not a guaranteed loan date** for an individual buyer
nodes.body: The agency's implementation deadline does not specify when each buyer will receive financing. Bond issuance and investor participation affect the program's rollout.

edges.why: The supplied guide contains no opposing ballot argument, not evidence that nobody objects.
The loan can replace part of the cash buyers otherwise need up front.
The relative cost of these loans is unknown.
Keeping interest low must coexist with covering the program's obligations.
Restricting assistance to first purchases of new or converted homes directs demand toward added housing.
Whether the program increases construction is not yet known.
The fiscal conclusion specifies no direct state or local costs.
Construction accountability includes altered procedures for homeowner claims.
The construction response underlying the jobs claim is uncertain.
These loans would join existing assistance options rather than create the first such assistance.
